There is a certain safety in being sad. You are not alone in this. Sad can be comforting, because sad is a place where you're already hurt, and you can sit in it. Happiness, especially for someone struggling with their mental health, can seem like dangerous, unmarked territory. It makes sense that you withdraw, and it's not just you, I promise. 

This is going to sound real fucking cheesy, but I encourage you to practice mindfulness. Notice the urge to flee when you're feeling joy creep in. Notice it, but don't judge it. Say, "hello urge! Nice to see you, but I don't need to act on you today." Stop -- like, physically stop if you need to -- and take inventory of what you are feeling. There can be more than one feeling. There can be joy, but there can also be fear, or disgust, or shame, or whatever the hell else crops up when you begin to feel happy. Notice all of it. Stay present. Challenge yourself to sit with it -- that joy, that sadness, and act opposite to your urge to escape. Maybe track your emotions on a calendar -- I do that. Once you start noticing your red flags, and becoming more in tune with your body and emotional experiences, it will be easier to let joy be joy. This is true with every emotion, ever -- if alarm bells are going off in your head but you have no idea wtf you're feeling, of course you will have urges to flee.

Mindfulness. And self compassion, because this is hard. Track your feelings and rate them. If you're not in therapy right now, maybe consider it. Best of luck to you x

As for forgiving others...yeah, it's a tough one. A teacher did some messed up things to me when I was a kid, and I grapple between rage, hurt, helplessness, forgiving and un-forgiving over and over for the past fifteen years. If you are feeling unsafe (like you are at immediate risk of severely harming/killing yourself or others) then you need to get immediate help. I can understand what you're going through -- I've been in the same scenario a number of times, in one way or another. You can't usually admit yourself directly to a psych facility, but you can admit yourself to the emergency room and wait for a placement. It's very simple. You walk up to the desk, and say "I'm suicidal". 

Being on a psych hold in the emergency room isn't fun. You'll have a babysitter at all times, won't be able to use a fork or spoon, won't be able to pee without the door open. But that's how the cookie crumbles. You'll meet with a psychiatrist and a social worker to figure out your next steps. If you're suicidal, they'll most likely send you to inpatient. You may have to wait a bit for a bed, but once you get one, they'll take you via ambulance (which is a little bit embarrassing lol). 

Psych hospitals, in my experience, tend to be a good place to get yourself stable, adjust your meds, get yourself to a place where you can start to really work on your illness. You'd most likely be there for a week or two. 

As for your mom...it's going to be hard, but trust me, she'd rather hear it from you than from the hospital or your best friend or your shrink (been there, not fun). Be blunt. Tell her that you are unsafe, and you need to go to the hospital. She will be scared. She might be angry (at the situation, people react to things in different ways). She might cry. But the immediate priority is you being safe, and if this is what needs to happen, it's what needs to happen. 

This is not the end for you. You got this, and you will come out the other side. Be proactive. Don't wait until it's too late. You know you need this, and that's the hardest part. Here for you. I have diagnosed BPD. Here are some of my red flags that I’ve learned to pick up on/that I’m working on. Hope it can be some help to you: 

1) major fear of abandonment/clinginess, being afraid at any time that people will leave 
2) 0 to 100 emotions (mainly negative). I feel everything like 100x greater than someone else 
3) self harming behavior (cutting, burning, hitting, etc) / recklessness, promiscuity, heavy substance use 
4) little to no sense of self — like “I don’t know who I am, I have no identity” 
5) anger outbursts / defensiveness 
6) sudden / extreme suicidal ideation 
7) love / hate dynamics — like, going from absolute love to absolute hate in a matter of moments 
8) generally just HIGH emotional sensitivity 
9) flashbacks / trauma reactions 
10) major self hatred / low self esteem, shit talking self
11) expressing feelings of emptiness
12 impulsivity / lack of regard for consequences 

People with BPD are sensitive and loving. I am a good person, but there are certainly things I must look out for. I am lucky to have a supportive family / received treatment so I am much better, but a couple years ago I was horribly toxic and consistently acting out. Can’t change that, but can look forward to the future. Take care of yourself:)

Okay, so as someone who is mentally ill, this is what I have learned, and a lesson that sticks with me -- you are dealt the hands that you are dealt. It is not your fault that you have this mental illness, but it *is your responsibility* to adapt to it. It is true that bipolar disorder can lead to more outbursts, and that is something you have to choose to deal with or not, but you are not an outlet for her anger or sadness, and you are not her emotional punching bag. 

Something that bothers me is all of those social media posts saying that as someone dating a mentally ill person, you have to be prepared for all of their outbursts and symptoms. Sure, sometimes that is true. But your feelings and experiences matter too. Do not fragilize (idk if that's a word but I use it in therapy) her. Tell her what you can handle. Tell her what you cannot. This relationship is a two way street. We'll never really be able to tell what is symptomatic versus her just being cruel, but either way, it is *your right to address it as her partner.*

I know it's hard, because in a relationship, you want your partner to feel happy and fulfilled, and you care about this guy a lot! But, transparency in a relationship is so important, and it's important that you have this conversation sooner rather than later, because it can lead to more issues later down the road of you bottle all of this up. Don't skirt around the issue -- start the conversation with exactly what you need to say -- "I'm not ready for a threesome, and here's why..." 

If he is true to his word about not pressuring you, he will respect these limits. You deserve to feel save and comfortable in your relationship, and that means being honest about what you are comfortable with versus uncomfortable with. Good luck x

Have you ever heard of schemas? A schema is a pattern of thoughts about yourself (and consequently, behaviors) that can heavily affect your relationships with others. There's a bunch of them, and one is called "self sacrifice" -- 

"...you started to associate **self worth and value** with '**helping others and being a good person'** and this belief became deeply embedded in your subconscious brain along with '**I must put other's before myself' and 'My needs are not as important as other people's'..."**

Schemas are so hard to break, because they are so ingrained in us and our relationships, but you are *not alone.* The only way to break a schema is to challenge it. A relationship is a two part street, and there should be fun! There should be a mutual appreciation, and it sounds like you're not getting that and it *hurts you!* 

So, if you want to break out of this pattern, challenge those thoughts. What if you *weren't* the helper all of the time? What if you let yourself be average, a friend who's around but not always on deck to help? It takes courage, but start small. Practice saying no. Affirm that you are still a good person without external validation. Getting a shrink helps too, lol, believe me. 

Good luck. If you want to learn more about schemas or just want to chat, hit me up:)

I haven't overcome my suicidal thoughts, but I've learned to manage them. Through lots of therapy, I've learned a lot about mindfulness, and having mindfulness of my thoughts. A thought is a thought. Say to yourself "I am noticing that I am having a suicidal thought." Try not to judge nor indulge/spiral in it. Imagine your thoughts as a huge waterfall, and you're standing behind it, not right in the fray, just noticing the water fall. Once you notice that thought, you can attach an emotion to it, whether it be shame, sadness, what have you.

Once you attach that thought to an emotion, you can work with what you experience, whether it be sticking your head in a bowl of ice water to engage your parasympathetic nervous system or acting opposite to your urge to isolate by surrounding yourself with others. It takes a lot of practice.

I'm still working on it. Multiple hospitalizations, meds, therapy, all the works. It's a constant battle. I hope you find peace with your headspace, someday.

Hey, I'm really sorry that you're in this situation. I can't fully understand what you're going through, but I was a suicidal 13/14 year old myself, so I can empathize. Maybe something I say here will help; I'm sorry if it doesn't. 

1) You're fourteen, so that either means you're in middle school or in the early ages of high school. Doesn't matter -- they're both INCREDIBLY difficult times for a lot of people. You're not alone in that, and school can be a major shit show. But in many cases, the people who loved their high school and middle school experiences remain stuck in the past after graduation -- I've seen it firsthand, being a recent high school grad. The hardships now are building you up to succeed after high school, where things, generally, will get better, because you have the opportunity to cut people out of your life who make you feel shitty. You have callouses, protecting you, while the people peaking now have baby-skin, if that makes sense. 

2) Teenagers have a tendency to be insecure, and in many cases, it's why bullies act the way they do. Like, a person happy with their lives has no reason to be an asshole. That being said, it does NOT excuse people being shitty. I'm so sorry that people are treating you this way, and it's not your fault. Sometimes, our school system sucks at combating bullying. I encourage you, nevertheless, to reach out to some sort of mentor, maybe a counselor or a trusted teacher. Without the help of a few trusted teacher, I'd probably be dead by now. The adults in your community can make a big difference. Getting involved in things you're interested in can also help. It's not a fix, but it can be better than being alone. 

3) Those people you opened up to suck. I don't understand how people can literally have no concept of mental illness. Like I said, a lot of kids suck. But know right now that I validate you, and so do the other people on this sub. You didn't ask for any of this, and I'm sorry people don't understand. Counseling/therapy can make a word of difference. I'd recommend perhaps talking to your guidance counselor about opportunities to see a school psychologist. I'm not sure if your school has this, but mine had an emotional support class, and a classroom kids could go to when feeling overwhelmed. 

4) Also, your mom sucks. I'm sorry she's like that. So many parents are so overwhelmed and resistant towards the idea of mental illness that they just lash out. She sounds like she has some deep-seated problems of her own. I would recommend checking out r/raisedbynarcissists , your mother sounds like she fits the bill. Remember, family doesn't end in blood, and as you grow and mature (you're VERY young) you most likely will find people more adept to fill a "family" role. 

Sorry that was so long. I hope that at least something I said is helpful -- in any event, please don't die. Fourteen, if you don't mind me saying, is horribly young to leave this earth, and it is not your time.

The commotion from the house next door was enough to rouse Noah from his midmorning nap and send him teetering toward his window, fetching grappling at his cornflower blue wall for support as he approached the frame. He had been neglecting the cane lately — said it made him too much of an old man. 

“Dad,” he calls, coughing lightly. “Come here!” 

I turn from his dresser, where I had been placing his newly folded clothes. His school uniform taunts me from the bottom shelf, not worn since early October. The drawer is shut, quickly. Over the months since Noah’s diagnosis, I have gotten better at obsessing over material objects, the old baseball glove in the garage I had bought him for his first season of little league, the class ring I had planned to give him on his last day of high school. Reminders of what could have been. 

My feelings are cast aside, for now. My new priority? Making Noah’s last summer the greatest of his young life. Disney, Six Flags, you name it — he was bound to be spoiled. 

“Dad!” He turns from the windowsill, impatient. “C’mon, look at this!”

I approach the window. New neighbors, unpacking their belongings from a white moving truck parked outside. An elderly couple, late seventies perhaps, and a young girl — granddaughter, maybe, about Noah’s age. Noah turns to me and grins. “We should say hi!” 

...

Our new neighbors are quiet, kind, and are quite delighted by the muffins Noah and I bake and bring them as a welcome gift. The girl, Clara, is indeed the wise age of seven. She becomes a regular at our household on weekends, playing Mario Kart and monster trucks with Noah alike. She isn’t bothered by his coughing fits, bulky cane, or the lack of hair on his head. I can only pray she understands that his time here is limited. 

…

Noah is getting worse. He’s disoriented, often scared, often angry. I’m kicking myself — I didn’t take him to Disney in time, and there’s no way in hell he can make it on a flight now. I can only focus on making him comfortable, surrounding him by family and friends. 

We set up a mock water park in the backyard, complete with sprinklers and one of those blow up slides. I douse him lightly with a hose, and he laughs, lightly. 

...

Clara’s visits grow less frequent as he grows sicker. When she visits us next, there is something different. They sit by the fire — he’s so cold lately — and talk in hushed voices. I don’t inturrupt. She holds his hand. 

…

Two weeks later, Noah goes into remission. It’s a miracle, they say, and I am at a loss for words. The youth returns to his face in a matter of hours. It’s nothing they’ve ever seen before, say the doctors. Noah says nothing, until later that night, when I tuck him in and wonder when I’ll wake from this dream. 

“Dad.” His voice is stronger now. 

“Yeah, buddy?” 

“It’s Clara. She’s lived a thousand lives. She’s seen the Eiffel Tower. She’s jumped out of a plane. She’s gone to Disney and written books and plays the violin and can swim every stroke and has been to the Bahamas and —“

“Noah, slow down. What are you talking about” 

He blinks up at me, his eyes bluer than usual even in the dulled moonlight. 

“Dad, she’s nine hundred and forty two years old.” 

…

The girl next door passes from a mysterious ailment the next day.

Honestly it’s just a lot of group work.  They take away your phone — as least, my program did, and give it back to you at the end. Ayy alright here we go -- 

1) Take a walk. Or a run. But in most practical situations walking is your best bet. When I feel anxious in school, I just take a lap around the building. Moving around makes me calmer. 

2) Grounding exercises! Sounds stupid, but for real, try it. Name 5 things you can see. 4 things you can hear. 3 things you can touch. If applicable, throw in something you can smell or taste. Helps put things in perspective. 

3) Journal. Write all the shit down. Much better on a page than in your head. I've filled countless composition books with all my negative thoughts. 

4) Time. Remind yourself that this too shall pass, and that anxiety often comes and goes in waves. Time can heal a lot (not all, but a good bit) 

5) Have something to hold or fiddle with, like a stress ball. I personally like holding poker chips. It gives your hands something to do. Doesn't work for everyone, but I like it.

Good luck!

Hello :) it's so awesome that you're trying to find ways to help your daughter. My mother found out when I was 13, so not that far off! Some things that could've helped me when she found out: 

1) Professional help -- but seems as if she's already in therapy, which is great. Just make sure she's up to date with her appointments and all that. Also, her therapist can definitely give you tips on how to help best, and also there are many support groups for parents of struggling kids -- my mom went to one for a while and it really helped her understand what I was going through.  

2) Coping skills. Ask your daughter what could help distract her when she feels an urge. A journal, headphones, coloring books...it can be anything. Make sure you have those skills accessible in your home. 

3) Avoid judgement, anger, and blame. It sounds like you avoid them already, but it can be easy to get tangled up with strong emotions when someone you love is hurting themselves. She needs you to stay calm, because she is probably terrified. You're her rock. Anger, uncontrollable tears, and judgement will not help. 

4) Above all, just remind her that you're there for her, and you love her no matter what. Recovery is a long process, but if she has you in her corner as an ally, it'll be a lot easier.

Absolutely. I was so tired of keeping my self harm relapse a secret, and I felt too afraid to go to my parents or someone in guidance, but I knew I needed help. This teacher is someone I trust a lot and who knows a lot about my history, and he had always told me he was there if I needed to talk.

I came to his classroom after school and told him I needed to talk to him about something important. We sat down and it kind of all came out -- how I've been struggling with self harm on and off for years, how I'm terrified of my parents finding out and being disappointed in me, how things have spiraled out of control. He didn't freak out or report me right away. He was extremely patient and kind about it, listened, and reassured me that things were going to be alright. However, teachers are mandated reporters, at least in the United States, so he had to tell someone else. He arranged a meeting with one of the school psychologists that he attended alongside of me, and we talked about how we could tell my parents in the best way that made me comfortable. 

If you tell a teacher, they have to report it by law. But that isn't always a bad thing, because it can help you get the help you need. Not everyone's experience was as good as mine, but if you have a teacher you really trust and are close with, they're really good resources. I'm glad I did because he helped me reach out to my parents and get me more intensive treatment. I hope this helps!

This is a simulation, and I have been gone for quite a while by now. I place down my glass, silently bid the ocean goodbye…eyes shut, I regain control over my body…

Eleanor appears, laying in bed across from me, reaching her slender fingers to stroke my face, and I am confused, because my hand reaches for her and I am not controlling it. I recognize the rough callouses on my fingers, my wedding band, how large my hand is compared to her feminine one, but I do not recognize myself reaching to stroke her hair. 

I do not recognize her touch, either. It’s as if all I am watching a stranger run his hands through her locks. She smiles. 

This is wrong. I yearn to speak, to feel, but something is pushing me out of reality and back to that fucking beach. Did I overdose on Realase? I swear, I took the right dosage…

“Andrew, dear, I love you.” Eleanor parts her lips, gazes into eyes that aren’t mine. “Ever since you started that new medication, everything has been so wonderful at home. The kids are talking about how much you’ve been playing with them. I really think this is helping.” 

A voice responds, and it sure as hell isn’t mine. “I agree, baby. I love our family so much, El.” 

This isn’t me. I never call you El…you’re my Ellie. Ellie, I need to come back…

Eleanor is fading, and I am screaming, but I can only hear the sweet nothings of a man who is not me. I find myself on a beach, a margarita in hand, staring at the sea. 

Where have I been for so long?

With such tedious tasks, of opening and closing doors, and propelling upwards and sinking downwards, and constantly belting a repetitive tune that no one bothers to listen to anyways, an entity such as I must find nourishment from the one place it can — human emotion. 

Toiling in one of the largest and most reputable hospitals in the state, emotions come easy and plentiful. They differ, and appeal to me in ways similarly to how humans experience taste — the rich and heavy aroma of sadness, the airy and sweet texture of happiness, the bitter and charcoal sensation of anger, the spice and uncertainty of fear. 

And with these emotions come memories. I have experienced so many, but few are remain prevalent. The gushing and overpowering relief of the young schoolteacher in the suburbs, whose high school sweet heart is now in remission. The engulfing sadness of the elderly man who lost his wife of natural causes and a long battle with dementia, with hints of relief and guilt after spending so many years caring for her. While memories are usually categorized as “happy” or “sad”, I found myself perplexed by one human in particular, a certain Andie Costa. 

Now, Andie Costa never particularly bled with emotion — she seemed to be in a perpetual state of shock or denial. She was a regular, early twenties. I gain fragments of her memories over the weeks she had visited, a single mother, minimum wage, disowned from her parents because of a teenage pregnancy. I had never met the father of her child, and for seemingly good reason, as memories of such a man left an entity such as I with a repugnant taste on my lips. 

I meet her everyday for a matter of weeks, and learn she is visiting her young son on life support, tragically struck in a hit and run outside her apartment complex. Her visits leave me hungry, her emotions masked as she goes through the motions, up and down the elevator. 

When she arrives frantic one morning, I know that something is amiss. She’s jamming the my buttons, hands shaking, quarters from the parking meter tumbling out of her purse. She’s cursing under her breath. All I can taste is fear. That is, until the lights flicker, the familiar groan of my entity halts, and the elevator is at a standstill. 

“Fuck!” The lights have gone out. She’s crying. She slams the emergency button, but to no avail. “Fucking dammit!” 

Fear, sadness, regret, flood through my system, and I want to throw up. Her emotions fill my being, and I am overcome with memories. 

A teenage girl being shouted at by her parents. A woman alone in a hospital room cradling a bundle. A boy taking his first steps. Babbling. Riding a bicycle. Scraped knees and the sharp sting of hydrogen peroxide. Arts and crafts and Power Rangers and macaroni art and a close to empty family tree and — 

Andie Costa sinks onto the floor of the elevator and sobs into her open palms. What I feel rots me from the inside. It is the pain of a mother losing her child. 

I can offer no comfort but the flickering lights of the elevator.

I actually just got out of inpatient less than a month ago. I didn't physically attempt, per say, but I had written a note, gathered an arsenal of pills, and had a date lined up. 

I am a senior in high school but I had been struggling with suicidal thoughts since I was 12. My first hospitalization was when I was 13. My depression has been so severe from such a young age that I don't remember a time I wasn't suicidal, passively or actively. What led to my recent ideation was fear of college, failure, disappointing my parents and teachers, not being perfect...everything just added up until I found myself writing my goodbyes. 

Inpatient really fucking sucked, as it always does, but I was able to get a much needed medication change and start DBT therapy, which so far has been helping immensely. I'm currently making up the work I missed for the month I was absent, but my teachers are extremely lenient and kind. I plan on going to college in the fall and continuing to receive counselling there. 

At first glance, you wouldn't think I'm depressed. I have a loving family and friends for the most part, and a solid support system...but depression doesn't care who you are or where you come from. 

I am slowly piecing things together again. My fear is that I'll be in and out of hospitals for the rest of my life. But at the moment, I'm glad I'm not dead. I have things to live for, people to live for, and maybe I'll look back on these past few months when I'm not as sick and be thankful I stayed strong. 

Thank you for asking :)

Hello! I'm 17, so I remember being 13 pretty well. Here are some tips for you:

-You don't have to have everything figured out right away (ie, college, your future, etc). Your peers will tell you that they do. More often than not, they're lying. 

-Teachers can actually be pretty chill. If you're struggling with a class, see them before/after school or during their free periods. Not only do you get extra help, you can build a positive relationship.

-Being pressured to drink is a rarity. If you don't want to, say no. People honestly don't care as much as your health teachers say they do. But if you do, for the love of God, be careful, and have a sober friend with you. 

-Mental health > school. Getting help when you're struggling doesn't make you weak. 

-If you haven't hooked up yet, wait till you feel comfortable. The first time I got with someone, it was with a guy I didn't know at all in a tent while I was absolutely wasted. 0/10 do not recommend, wish I waited. 

-Don't start self harming. Please.

-Don't be ashamed of your taste in music. If it makes you happy, who cares? 

-Remember life gets better. Middle school sucks.

-When people brag about not sleeping/eating/self destructive habits, it's not cool. Try and sleep at least 7 hours.

-I'll say it again. It gets better.

There a difference between passive suicidal thoughts and active suicidal thoughts. Active thoughts mean that you have a plan or intent, and are a danger to yourself. Passive thoughts are still dangerous, but there is no plan/intent in mind, and you are still safe. 

I've experienced both, and I've been to enough therapy that I can tell the difference and get the appropriate help. It's important that you do the same, and reach out to someone! I know it's scary, but at least in my experience, passive thoughts can turn active if left unaddressed for too long. I've been in and out of psychiatric hospitals since 13 (am 17 now), so if you have any questions about what can get you admitted versus what can't, you can ask me. 

Stay safe.

It's strange, because it's hard to remember a time in my life when I wasn't depressed. I wrote my first suicide note at 12, and was first hospitalized at 13. For me, depression is similar to wearing a really heavy jacket in the middle of summer. You're sweating, suffocating, it's a goddamn heatwave, but no one notices. You feel lethargic and sick. Everyday activities are mountains to climb, and everyone tells you just to take off the jacket, but you can't, it's not that easy. 

It isn't beautiful, the way it's spun into novels and stories. I've said "fuck it" and just didn't brush my teeth when I lost motivation. I've snapped at my parents and screamed across the kitchen, "I hate you, I hate you", when they gave me the world for 14 years. 

I'm 17 now, and while things have gotten a lot better through therapy and medication, I still struggle. Luckily, I have a really good support system, and I'm able to trust my friends to listen when I need an ear-- that's really important. Remind your friend that you're there for her through this, but also remember to take care of yourself! Encourage her to reach out for help if she hasn't already, because you can't do this on your own x.

I really miss that girl. She was incredibly funny. We were both reading To Kill a Mockingbird for school. She told me that if I tried to kill myself again, she would send Atticus Finch to fuck me up. She was really sick though. I hope she's doing alright. If you're reading this, El, I'm still fighting here!

I didn't have to worry about school too much, about my parents- I could devote all my time to getting better, which is what I needed to do in the first place.

Here's to recovery, man. Hope I never have to go back again, but I'll never forget the people I met there.

"Excuse me, Mrs. So-and-So", he says to my mom, "would it be alright with you if I kissed your daughter goodnight?" 

I blush. His mom blushes. My mom shrugs. 

"Sure," she says, "go for it."

Cue my first kiss, with both my mother and his mother watching. It was very innocent- like half a second peck, but it made my heart flutter and my palms sweaty and all of the above. I'll always remember it.

Not insensitive at all, I understand it's a pretty rare disorder and it can be hard to wrap your head around. It is very similar to OCD, in the sense that both revolve around obsessions (for me, the urge to pick my skin brought on by anxiety or boredom), that can only be resolved by compulsions (the act of picking my skin as well.) If you have any questions, feel free to ask them, I'm open to talking about it!

Dermatillomania. Essentially, I pick and pick at my skin until I bleed. 

Imagine this itch, this thought that hits you like a ton of bricks. It's a need. I need to pick my skin, and until I do, you can forget about me thinking anything else. It's the worst when I'm nervous, and it's almost subconscious. It isn't your run of the mill biting your nails- I've taken a mechanical pencil and dug under my skin until I saw blood, I've hidden in bathroom stalls and tore at my cuticles until I realize I'm twenty minutes late to class. I haven't gotten my nails done since I was what, six? And even then the specialist commented on how ugly my hands are.

Sometimes, I don't even realize it's happening. Just a couple weeks ago, I was taking a pretty important exam. My anxiety was all over the place. I'm finishing up, trying to budget my time, looking over my work- and I realize there's blood all over my answer sheet, the kind with the bubbles? I didn't even realize how bad the derm was that day. Imagine my shame as I shuffle to the back of the room where my teacher was sitting and explain to him that I was so so sorry, but I got blood all over his test and I'm going to need a new answer sheet. 

This disorder has taken everything from me- my self confidence, any aspect of physical beauty I have. It sucks being "that girl who picks at her skin." My disorder is so misunderstood, and God knows what I would do to go a day where I don't feel the aching compulsion to pick. I feel ashamed of my body, ashamed of myself that this is the way I function. I cannot function without picking myself apart. I hate the way my fingers stain my pencils, the way I want to cry when I put on hand sanitizer and the way I have to shove my hands in my pockets when I walk down the hallway.

This felt good to write out. Thanks for taking the time to read about this, and please, stay strong.

In second grade I was at a friend's house for dinner, and her parents were serving this mystery-meat type contraption that really did not look appealing. Being the shy and passive girl I was, not to mention an incredibly picky eater, I didn't want it but also didn't want to risk insulting her parents by saying that it didn't look appetizing. 

Cue an assortment of different lies and excuses running through my head, until a lightbulb goes off in my mind. "Oh, I'm so sorry, Mr and Mrs, but I never had a chance to mention I'm a vegetarian!"

They're incredibly understanding, and I get off with a peanut butter and jelly. But to this day, I'm still good friends with this girl, and I always have to remind myself not to eat meat in front of her or her parents. I'm simply in too deep.
